736.title: Not yet
736.hook: Ananda was still unawakened when the Buddha died, and wept
736.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, a sekha or learner is a disciple who has entered the path but not completed it, and Ananda's story is told to encourage practitioners who are still on the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, water from the well, and your line: I asked for water. Whose kindness did you take gladly? Today, a long night for Ananda, and what he still hadn't reached. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

Night, in a grove of sal trees at Kusinara. The Buddha is dying. Around him are monks of every kind: some, the texts say, fully free, and some still on the way. Ananda is among the second group. He has been at the teacher's side for many years, and kept what he heard. And he is not yet awakened. Earlier on this path we watched him slip away to weep in a doorway, and the Buddha call him back. Today, let's stay with those two words that sit under the whole scene: not yet.
screen: `A GROVE AT KUSINARA.` → `SOME FREE, SOME ON THE WAY.` → `NOT YET.`

segments.voice: First, the start, long before. In the Samyutta Nikaya, Ananda remembers that when he was newly ordained, a monk named Punna taught him, and hearing it, he broke through to the teaching. So Ananda had entered the path early. He wasn't a beginner on this night. He was a learner. Second, the learner at the end. The Pali word is sekha: one still in training, on the path but not at its end. In the doorway, Ananda says it of himself, in paraphrase: I'm still a learner, with work left to do, and my teacher, who was so kind to me, is passing away. And the Buddha doesn't call that failure. He tells Ananda he has served him well, and says: keep at it, and you'll soon be free. Soon. Not now. Third, the night itself. When the Buddha passes, the discourse says some monks weep and some bear it calmly: everything made comes apart. Ananda speaks a verse about the shock of that moment. And then, the text says, Anuruddha, one of the monks already free, and Ananda spent the rest of that night together, talking about the teaching. The finished one and the unfinished one, side by side until morning. Nobody sent the learner away. Fourth, what not yet means. It isn't never. In the texts, the learner is already on the path and counted among the noble disciples. Ananda had kept what he heard, served his teacher faithfully, and still wasn't done, and the story treats that as a place to stand rather than a verdict. Tomorrow we'll see how not yet ended.
screen: `A START, LONG BEFORE.` · `STILL A LEARNER AT THE END.` · `A NIGHT OF TALK WITH ANURUDDHA.` · `NOT YET ISN'T NEVER.` · then, large: `NOT YET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with yourself. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing in your life that's still not finished. A habit you're still working on. A skill. A grief. Something you thought you'd have sorted by now. Say it plainly to yourself, and then add two words: not yet. Notice what changes when you say not yet instead of never. Then, the way the Buddha did for Ananda, name one thing you have already done well. Hold both. Rest with the breath until the end. The bell holds the time.
Not yet. When the Buddha died, Ananda was still a learner, on the path and not at its end, and he wept; the Buddha's word for him was soon. Today's word.
Your line: not yet. Today, when you catch yourself saying I'll never get this, change it, out loud if you can, to not yet. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

737.title: Between standing and lying
737.hook: the night before the council, Ananda gives up striving, lies down, and is freed before his head reaches the pillow (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
737.howItsDone: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions tell Ananda's last night as a story about balanced effort, and recall it for students whose practice has grown tight and forced.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the teacher had died, and Ananda wept, still unawakened. Your line was not yet. Were you patient with yourself somewhere, even once? Tonight the council is one day away, and Ananda is still not there. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

A deadline, and a sacred one. The elders are gathering at Rajagaha to recite the teaching together, and in the Vinaya's account every one of them has already reached the end of the path. Every one except Ananda. He's the man who walked beside the Buddha, carried his water, heard the discourses day after day. And he hasn't arrived. So on the last night he does the obvious thing with a deadline. He works. He practices hard, attending to the body, hour after hour, pushing at a door that won't open. Then, toward dawn, he stops pushing. He decides to lie down. Today is about what happens in that small space, between standing and lying.
screen: `A COUNCIL TOMORROW.` → `EVERYONE ARRIVED BUT ONE.` → `HE PUSHES ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the push. The Vinaya says Ananda spent much of that night in mindfulness of the body. This isn't a lazy man looking for a shortcut. It's a careful one, doing the practice the way he was taught. And still, by effort alone, nothing gives. Second, the letting go. Toward dawn he thinks: let me lie down. He isn't quitting the path. He's setting down the strain. A later commentary adds a reason. It says he saw that his effort had grown too tight, and he eased it. Third, the moment itself. He leans his body toward the bed. And the text says that before his head reached the pillow, and while his feet had not yet left the ground, his mind was freed. Not sitting. Not walking. Not lying down. Somewhere in between. It's a detail worth staying with: the thing he had chased for so long came in a moment that doesn't even have a name. Fourth, what it says to an ordinary evening. Ananda didn't stop practicing. He had practiced for a long time, and that practice was the ground under his feet. What he stopped was the clutching. The story doesn't say effort is useless. It says effort can tighten into a fist, and a closed fist can't receive anything. In the morning, the account goes on, he took his place among the elders as one of them.
screen: `HE PUSHED ALL NIGHT.` · `HE LET GO, AND LAY DOWN.` · `BEFORE HIS HEAD TOUCHED THE PILLOW.` · `EFFORT, WITHOUT THE FIST.` · then, large: `BETWEEN STANDING AND LYING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop straining, for once. Settle where you are, and notice where you're pushing right now. The jaw. The shoulders. The space between the eyebrows. Maybe even the breath, being managed. Let one of those go, the way Ananda let himself lie down. You're not giving anything up. You're only setting down the extra. If you catch yourself working hard at relaxing, notice that too, and smile at it. Then stay with the breath as it is, without trying to improve it. The bell holds the time.
Between standing and lying. The night before the council, Ananda sets down the strain, lies down, and is freed before his head reaches the pillow. Today's word.

Your line: between standing and lying. Today, when you catch yourself straining at something that won't move, put it down for one breath, and see what comes into the gap. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

738.title: The recital
738.hook: at the first council Mahakassapa asks and Ananda answers: where each discourse was spoken, and to whom (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
738.tomorrow: The couple who didn't want to marry
738.howItsDone: Monks and nuns in Theravada communities still learn discourses and verses by heart and chant them together, and the recitation of texts is a regular part of monastery life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, between standing and lying: Ananda set down the strain and was freed before his head touched the pillow. Did you put one strain down, even for a breath? This morning he walks into the council. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

One elder asks. One elder answers. The teacher who spoke these words is gone. And a room full of elders at Rajagaha has one job: make sure what he said doesn't drift away. So the Vinaya describes something like a very calm exam. Mahakassapa, presiding, asks questions. Ananda answers. And everyone else listens closely, because once the answers are agreed, this is the teaching they will carry. It all rests on one man's memory, and on a room willing to check it. Today, the recital.

First, the questions. They aren't about doctrine first. They're about place and people. In the Vinaya's account Kassapa asks: where was the discourse called the Net of Brahma spoken? Ananda answers: on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, at the king's rest house in Ambalatthika. And about whom? About a wanderer named Suppiya and a young brahmin, his pupil. Then the next discourse, and the next, through the collections. Second, why place and people. A teaching remembered with its setting is harder to bend. If you know who was standing there and what they asked, you know what the answer was answering. It may be part of why the discourses begin where they do, with a town, a grove, a person. Third, an honest gap. During the council Ananda also reports something the Buddha told him near the end: that after he was gone the community could drop the lesser and minor rules. The elders ask which ones those are. And Ananda has to say he didn't ask. The council talks it over, and Kassapa proposes they keep every rule as it was, and the elders agree. A good memory, it turns out, also remembers what it never got. Fourth, the room. Ananda recited, but he didn't recite alone in the end. Tradition says the elders chanted it back together, and that from then on the teaching lived in voices: groups of monks carrying it, generation after generation, reciting it aloud. One man remembered. A whole room made sure the memory held.
screen: `WHERE WAS IT SPOKEN? TO WHOM?` · `A SETTING KEEPS THE MEANING.` · `THE QUESTION HE NEVER ASKED.` · `A ROOM RECITES IT BACK.` · then, large: `HE REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite one verse by heart. Pick a line you'd like to carry, from any tradition you love, or try this one from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Say it slowly, three or four times, out loud if you can. Then close your eyes and say it without looking. Where you stumble, look once, and try again. When it holds, let it go quiet and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The recital. At the first council Kassapa asks where each discourse was spoken and to whom, and Ananda answers from memory. Today's word.
Your line: he remembered. Today, say your verse once more, somewhere ordinary, on the stairs or in the car, and notice that it's still there. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

739.title: The couple who didn't want to marry
739.word: The couple who didn't want to marry
739.hook: Pippali and Bhadda, both longing to leave the household life, are married anyway and live as friends (commentary on AN 1.14)
739.howItsDone: The story of Pippali and Bhadda is told in the Theravada commentaries as the early life of Mahakassapa and Bhadda Kapilani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the recital, and your line: he remembered. Is your verse still there when you reach for it? Today we leave Ananda and meet the elder who asked him the questions, long before he was an elder. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

A young man in a rich brahmin family is told it's time to marry. He doesn't want to. He wants to leave home for the holy life. But his parents keep pressing, so, the commentary says, he tries a clever way out. He has a statue of a woman made in gold, and announces he'll marry only someone who looks like that. Surely no such woman exists. The family's messengers carry the statue from town to town. And in a town called Sagala, they find her. Her name is Bhadda. And she doesn't want to marry either.
screen: `A SON WHO WON'T MARRY.` → `A GOLDEN STATUE.` → `THEY FIND HER ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: This is the story the commentaries tell of Pippali, who will become Mahakassapa, and Bhadda Kapilani. First, the letters. Each of them writes to the other: I hear we're to be married; find someone else; I mean to leave home. The story says the letters were stopped on the road and swapped for warmer ones, so neither plan worked. The two families got their wedding. Second, the wedding night. In the commentary they don't pretend. They talk, and find out they want the same thing. So they agree to live as companions, not as husband and wife. A garland of flowers lies on the bed between them, and the story says neither crossed it. Third, the long friendship. They run a large estate together and stay friends. The tradition doesn't present this as a sad or cold arrangement. It presents two people who understood each other, and kept faith with what they'd agreed. Fourth, the turn. One day, the story goes, Pippali watches birds eating the worms turned up by his plows, and Bhadda watches crows eating insects in the seeds laid out to dry. Each one feels the weight of the harm their wealth depends on. So they shave their heads, put on simple robes, take up clay bowls, and walk out of the house together, while the people of the estate weep at the door. Two who wanted to leave, and who waited, side by side, until they could. Where they went from there is a story for another day.
screen: `TWO LETTERS, SWAPPED ON THE ROAD.` · `A GARLAND BETWEEN THEM.` · `FRIENDS WHO RUN AN ESTATE.` · `THEY WALK OUT TOGETHER.` · then, large: `TWO WHO WANTED TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a friendship inside a marriage, or inside any close partnership. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a couple you know, your own if you have one, or your parents, or friends, or grandparents. Look past the roles, the bills and the schedule, and find the friendship underneath. One moment when they were clearly on the same side. Hold that moment for a while. If it's your own partnership, think of one thing you could say tonight that a friend would say. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The couple who didn't want to marry. Pippali and Bhadda, both longing to leave home, married anyway, lived as friends, and walked out together. Today's word.
screen: `THE COUPLE WHO DIDN'T WANT TO MARRY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: two who wanted to leave. Today, say one thing to someone close that a friend would say, not a manager or a parent. Just a friend. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

740.title: Exchanging robes
740.hook: the Buddha gives Kassapa his worn rag robes and takes Kassapa's soft patchwork cloak (SN 16.11)
740.howItsDone: In some Theravada forest monasteries monks still sew robes from donated or cast-off cloth and dye them by hand, and the story of the exchanged robes is told as the bond between the Buddha and Mahakassapa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pippali and Bhadda, two who wanted to leave, walked out of their house together. Did you say one thing to someone close the way a friend would? Today Pippali meets his teacher. Day seven hundred forty.

Years later, an old monk tells a story about the day he met the Buddha. In the discourse he's speaking to Ananda, and he's not in a sentimental mood. He's making a point. But the story he tells is tender anyway. He'd left home, he says, already wearing a robe, and set out looking for a teacher. On the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, at a shrine by the way, he saw the Buddha sitting. And he knew at once: this is my teacher. What happened next involved two pieces of cloth.
screen: `AN OLD MONK REMEMBERS.` → `A SHRINE BY THE ROAD.` → `THIS IS MY TEACHER.`

segments.voice: First, the seat. In the discourse, Kassapa bows and declares himself the Buddha's disciple. They walk on together for a while, and then the Buddha steps off the road to sit at the foot of a tree. Kassapa folds his own outer robe, a patchwork cloak, and lays it down as a seat for his teacher. Second, the remark. The Buddha sits on it and says, in effect: this patchwork cloak of yours is soft. That's all. A comment about cloth. And Kassapa hears what's underneath it, and offers the cloak as a gift. Third, the exchange. The Buddha accepts. And then he asks a question back: will you wear my rag robes, the worn-out hempen ones? These are robes made from cloth other people threw away. Kassapa says yes. The teacher takes the soft cloak, and the student takes the rough, worn one. Fourth, what Kassapa makes of it. Telling the story to Ananda, he says that if anyone could rightly be called the Buddha's true son, the heir to his worn rag robes, it would be him. He doesn't say the heir to his throne, or his teaching hall. The heir to his old clothes. The soft cloak is the easy thing to want. Kassapa treasured the worn one, because of whose it had been, and what it said: a life with few wants, chosen on purpose. Tomorrow we'll see how long he kept that choice.
screen: `A CLOAK FOLDED INTO A SEAT.` · `YOUR CLOAK IS SOFT.` · `WILL YOU WEAR MY RAG ROBES?` · `HEIR TO THE WORN ROBE.` · then, large: `THE WORN ROBE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear something humble. Settle, and breathe. Rest a hand on whatever you're wearing right now. Feel the cloth. Notice whether it's new or old, chosen to impress or chosen because it was clean. Then think of something you own that's worn, faded, mended, or plain, something you'd usually leave in the drawer. You don't need to give anything away. Just picture putting it on and walking out the door in it, the way Kassapa did. Notice what that stirs up. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Exchanging robes. Kassapa offers his soft patchwork cloak, and the Buddha gives him his own worn rag robes in return. Today's word.
Your line: the worn robe. Today, wear or use one plain, worn thing on purpose, and let it remind you how little you need. Day seven hundred forty.

741.title: The strict practices
741.hook: rag robes, alms food, living in the forest: the Buddha tells Kassapa he is old and may let them go, and Kassapa explains why he keeps them (SN 16.5)
741.howItsDone: In the Thai forest tradition and other Theravada communities, some monks take up dhutanga practices for a time or for life, such as eating one meal a day from the alms round or living in the forest, while others keep only the ordinary rules.

segments.voice: Yesterday, exchanging robes: Kassapa gave his soft cloak and took the Buddha's worn rag robes. Your line was the worn robe. What plain thing did you wear or use on purpose? Today, how long he kept wearing it. Day seven hundred forty-one.

The robes are heavy now. That's the first thing the Buddha says in this short discourse. Kassapa has grown old, and the hempen rag robes he's worn for so long hang heavy on him. So the Buddha makes a kind offer. You're old, Kassapa. Wear the robes householders give you. Accept meals when people invite you. Live near me, instead of out in the forest. Nobody would blame him. His teacher is giving him permission. And Kassapa, politely, says no.
screen: `THE ROBES ARE HEAVY NOW.` → `A KIND OFFER.` → `KASSAPA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, what he keeps. In the discourse Kassapa lists his way of life: a long time living in the forest, eating only what he receives on the alms round, wearing rag robes, keeping only the robes he needs, wanting little, content, secluded, putting in effort. And he says he praises these things to others too. Later tradition gathers practices like these under one name, dhutanga. Second, the name. In the Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa's long handbook, these are explained as practices of a monk who has shaken off the defilements. They're not required of anyone. They're chosen, on top of the ordinary rules, by those who want a sharper, simpler life. Third, his reasons. The Buddha asks him why he keeps them, and Kassapa gives two. One: they make for a pleasant life for him, here and now. He isn't suffering through them; he likes living this way. Two, and this is where today's line comes from: compassion for those who come later. He hopes that people in the future will look back and say, the disciples of the Buddha lived like this, and take heart, and try it too. Fourth, the answer. The Buddha says: good, good, Kassapa. You are practicing for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world. So an old man keeps carrying heavy robes, not to prove anything, and not because he has to, but so that someone he'll never meet can see that the path is still walked. For those to come.
screen: `FOREST, ALMS, RAG ROBES.` · `PRACTICES OF SHAKING OFF.` · `A PLEASANT LIFE, HERE AND NOW.` · `AN EXAMPLE FOR LATER PEOPLE.` · then, large: `FOR THOSE TO COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one simple practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small, plain habit you already keep, or once kept. A walk without the phone. Tea without a screen. Making your bed. Eating one meal slowly. Pick one. Now ask Kassapa's two questions about it. Does it make this life a little more pleasant, here and now? And who might see it, a child, a roommate, a friend, and quietly take it up? You don't need a big answer. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dhutanga. Simple, strict practices, like forest living, alms food and rag robes, taken up by choice; Kassapa keeps them into old age. Today's word.
Your line: for those to come. Today, keep your one simple practice where someone else might see it, and let that be a small gift to whoever comes next. Day seven hundred forty-one.

742.title: The leper's offering
742.hook: on his alms round Kassapa stands by a man with leprosy, accepts a lump of rice from his hand, and eats it (Theragatha, Mahakassapa's verses)
742.howItsDone: On the alms round in Theravada countries, monks walk in silence and receive whatever food is placed in the bowl, from any householder; Kassapa's verses about the leper's rice are one of the texts that show this way of receiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhutanga, the strict practices Kassapa kept into old age. Your line: for those to come. Did someone see your one simple practice? Today, one of those alms rounds. Day seven hundred forty-two.

Morning, and an old monk walks down from his lodging into town with his bowl. This is the alms round: you don't choose the food, and you don't choose the giver. You stand, and you receive what's offered. Today the one who wants to give is a man with leprosy, sitting and eating his own meal. Kassapa doesn't cross the street. He goes and stands beside him. And the man lifts a lump of rice in his damaged hand and puts it in the bowl. These lines are Kassapa's own, in the verses the tradition gives him. What he did next is today's story.
screen: `A BOWL, A MORNING ROUND.` → `HE STANDS BESIDE HIM.` → `RICE FROM A DAMAGED HAND.`

segments.voice: First, the offering. In the verses, the man's hand is so damaged by his illness that, as he places the food in the bowl, a finger falls in with it. The poem doesn't look away from that. And Kassapa is standing right beside him. Second, the eating. Kassapa says he sat down by a wall and ate that rice. And he adds the line that gives the story its force: while he was eating, and afterward, he felt no disgust. Third, why he tells it. These aren't boasting verses. They sit among lines about a simple life: food from the alms round, medicine from what others discard, a seat at the foot of a tree. For Kassapa, a gift is a gift. The giver isn't graded first. The man with leprosy got to do what the other householders did. He got to give, and be received. Fourth, what it isn't. The story isn't asking anyone to ignore illness or take risks with health. It's about what comes after a gift is taken: the quiet recoil, the polite thanks and the thing set aside later. The verses say none of that came, not while he ate and not afterward. He didn't only accept it. He ate it. And this closes a week of great disciples: Ananda's tears and his night between standing and lying, the recital, Pippali and Bhadda leaving together, the worn robe, the strict practices, and now a lump of rice from an unexpected hand.
screen: `A GIFT FROM A DAMAGED HAND.` · `HE ATE, AND FELT NO DISGUST.` · `THE GIVER ISN'T GRADED FIRST.` · `NO RECOIL, DURING OR AFTER.` · then, large: `HE ATE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept a gift without judging. Settle, and breathe. Think of a gift you accepted politely and then quietly set aside. A clumsy present still in its box. Advice you nodded at and never tried. A dish you praised and didn't finish. Hold that gift in your mind. What was actually offered? What would it take to use it, wear it, try it, the way Kassapa ate the rice? Let yourself receive it fully now. If thanks come up, let them come. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The leper's offering. On his alms round Kassapa stands beside a man with leprosy, accepts rice from his hand, and eats it without disgust. Today's word.

Your line: he ate it. Today, when someone offers you something, help, food or advice, don't stop at polite thanks. Use it, taste it, try it, and let the giver see it was received. Day seven hundred forty-two.

original.note: Pali dana, giving: the man's offering is dana, received like any other.

what it means: a gift is received all the way through, eaten and not set aside, with no disgust during or after.
what a scholar hears: the scene is in Mahakassapa's own verses in the Theragatha, set among lines about the simple needs of a monk.
